In particular for all
n

\raisebox{0.52205pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.47458pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.44444pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{686462}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{686462}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{686462}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{686462}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{p_{n}}}$}}}{\makebox[10.47458pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.44444pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{686462}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{686462}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{686462}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{686462}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{p_{n}}}$}}}{\makebox[9.02634pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.41112pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{591550}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{591550}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{591550}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{591550}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle p_{n}}}$}}}{\makebox[8.60254pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{1.72221pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{563776}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{563776}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{563776}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle p_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{563776}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle p_{n}}}$}}}}}\raisebox{0.52205pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset{\mathfrak{E}}
. Then as
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[7.86249pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{515276}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{515276}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{515276}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{515276}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{C}}$}}}{\makebox[7.86249pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{515276}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{515276}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{515276}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{515276}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{C}}$}}}{\makebox[6.22598pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{408026}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{408026}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{408026}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{408026}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle C}}$}}}{\makebox[5.3202pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{348665}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{348665}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{348665}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle C}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{348665}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle C}}$}}}}
is finite-stable, the sequence
(\mathpzc{p}_{n})
is finite. Contradiction.

•

Or
if
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}
is a path of
{\mathfrak{D}}
, i.e.,
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}\in C
,
\overline{\mathpzc{p}}
is a path of
{\mathfrak{E}}
but
\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}}
is not a path of
{\mathfrak{E}}
.
We have that
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}\in V_{{\mathbf{B}}}
, thus
\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}}\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\in{\mathbf{B}}
(corollary
4
). Thus contradiction as
{\mathfrak{E}}\in{\mathbf{B}}^{\perp}
.

•

Or
if
\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}
is a path of
{\mathfrak{E}}
,
\mathpzc{p}
is a path of
{\mathfrak{D}}
but
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}
is not a path of
{\mathfrak{D}}
.
Hence in particular
\kappa^{-}
is not present in
{\mathfrak{D}}
.
Furthermore
\mathpzc{p}
is a (positive-ended) prefix of
\left<{\mathfrak{D}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{E}}\right>
thus
\mathpzc{p}\in C
as a consequence of the first part of this proof. Then
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\in{\mathbf{B}}
(corollary
4
).
But
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}=\left<\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{E}}\right>
thus
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{B}}}
.
Thus
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
could be added to
C
, contradiction with the fact that
C
is a maximal clique.

Hence
{\mathfrak{D}}\in{\mathbf{B}}
. Suppose that
{\mathfrak{D}}\not\in|{\mathbf{B}}|
, then there exists a design
{\mathfrak{E}}\in{\mathbf{B}}
such that
{\mathfrak{E}}\subsetneq{\mathfrak{D}}
, i.e., there exists a path
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\in C
such that
\mathpzc{p}
is a path in
{\mathfrak{E}}
,
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}
is not a path in
{\mathfrak{E}}
. As
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\in C
, there exists a design
{\mathfrak{F}}\in{\mathbf{B}}^{\perp}
such that
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[26.91211pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{6.36983pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.36983pt}{$\resizebox{1763712}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.36983pt}{$\resizebox{1763712}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.36983pt}{$\resizebox{1763712}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.36983pt}{$\resizebox{1763712}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}$}}}{\makebox[26.91211pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{6.36983pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.36983pt}{$\resizebox{1763712}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.36983pt}{$\resizebox{1763712}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.36983pt}{$\resizebox{1763712}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.36983pt}{$\resizebox{1763712}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}$}}}{\makebox[22.2803pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.08095pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.08095pt}{$\resizebox{1460162}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.08095pt}{$\resizebox{1460162}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.08095pt}{$\resizebox{1460162}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.08095pt}{$\resizebox{1460162}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}$}}}{\makebox[20.52576pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82225pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82225pt}{$\resizebox{1345176}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82225pt}{$\resizebox{1345176}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82225pt}{$\resizebox{1345176}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82225pt}{$\resizebox{1345176}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}}$}}}}
is a path in
{\mathfrak{F}}
. Hence
{\mathfrak{E}}\not\perp{\mathfrak{F}}
, contradiction.

3.2.
Positive Saturation, Negative Saturation of a set of paths

Let us go
back to the initial question: let
S
be a set of legal paths, is
S
the set of visitable paths of a behaviour? We know from proposition
5
that we should base our analysis on the set of positively saturated maximal cliques of
S
. As suggested in example
3.2
, each path in
S
should be in some positively saturated maximal clique of
S
. Another condition, called
negative saturation
, should also be satisfied: a path
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
contained in the design generated by some positively saturated maximal clique should be in
S
as soon as the design
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
is orthogonal to all positively saturated maximal clique of
S
(see example
3.2
). Before that, we recall the following points: let
\mathpzc{m}\mathpzc{n}
be a visitable path with
\mathpzc{m}
positive-ended then
\mathpzc{m}
is also a visitable path, let
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}
be a visitable path then
\mathpzc{p}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
is also a visitable path. Hence a set
S
should be prefix and daimon closed:

{defi}

[Prefix closure, daimon closure]
Let
S
be a set of legal paths of same base:

•

S
is
prefix-closed
if all positive-ended prefix of an element of
S
is an element of
S
.

•

S
is
daimon-closed
if for all path
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}\in S
,
\mathpzc{p}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
.

{exa}

Let us first remark that each path in
S
should be in some positively saturated maximal clique of
S
.
Let
S
be the prefix and daimon closure of the two paths
\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}\kappa_{2}^{+}
and
\kappa^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
. We only have the following maximal cliques of
S
:

•

C_{0}=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}

•

C_{1}=\{\kappa^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}

•

C_{2}=\{\kappa^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}

•

C_{3}=\{\kappa^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}\kappa_{2}^{+}\}

Note that
C_{3}
is not positively saturated:
\kappa^{+}\in C_{3}
,
\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}\kappa_{2}^{+}\in C_{3}
,
\kappa^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
but
\kappa^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}\kappa_{2}^{+}\not\in S
. Thus there is no positively saturated maximal clique containing the path
\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}\kappa_{2}^{+}
. By the way
S
is not the set of visitable paths of some behaviour.

Let us now motivate the need for negative saturation. Let
S
be the set of paths
\{{\scriptstyle\maltese},\kappa^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}
:
S
is daimon and positive prefix closed. We have the following maximal cliques of
S
:

•

C_{0}=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}

•

C_{1}=\{\kappa^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}

•

C_{2}=\{\kappa^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+},\kappa^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}

Notice that these three cliques are positively saturated.
However the design
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{2}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
contains the path
\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
.
Remark that the design
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
is orthogonal to all three designs
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{i}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
but the path
\kappa^{+}\kappa_{1}^{-}\kappa_{1}^{+}\kappa_{2}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
is not in
S
.
Here too,
S
is not the set of visitable paths of some behaviour.

{defi}

[Positive saturation condition]
A set
S
of legal paths of same base is
positively saturated
if for each path
\mathpzc{p}\in S
, there exists a positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
S
such that
\mathpzc{p}\in C
.

In the following proposition, we remark that, if it exists, there is a standard positively saturated clique. This clique
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
is in fact the smallest positively saturated maximal clique containing a given path
\mathpzc{p}
.

Proposition 6
.

Let
S
be a set of legal paths of same base, prefix and daimon closed.
The three conditions are equivalent:

i)

S
is positively saturated.

ii)

For each path
\mathpzc{p}\in S
, the clique
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
defined below is positively saturated for
S
:

C_{\mathpzc{p}}=\{\mathpzc{q}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \mathpzc{q}\in S,\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\}\cup\{\mathpzc{w}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \mathpzc{w}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S,\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{w}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$},\raisebox{0.72041pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{w}\kappa^{-}}\raisebox{0.72041pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\not\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\}

iii)

For each path
\mathpzc{p}\in S
, there exists a positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
S
without infinite strictly increasing sequence and such that
\mathpzc{p}\in C
.

Proof 3.2
.

i)\Rightarrow ii)
Suppose that there exists a path
\mathpzc{p}\in S
such that
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
is not positively saturated.
This means that there exist two paths
\mathpzc{m}\in C_{\mathpzc{p}}
and
\mathpzc{n}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\in C_{\mathpzc{p}}
, such that
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
but
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\notin S
.
Note that
\kappa^{+}\neq{\scriptstyle\maltese}
. Note also that
\mathpzc{m}
cannot end with a daimon, otherwise
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}
is not a path. Therefore
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{m}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
and
\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{n}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}}\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
.
As
S
is positively saturated, there exists a positively saturated maximal clique
C
containing
\mathpzc{p}
, hence also
\mathpzc{m}
and
\mathpzc{n}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}
thus
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\in S
. Contradiction.

ii)\Rightarrow iii)
Let us remark that the clique
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
is a maximal clique of
S
. Indeed, let
\mathpzc{m}
be an element of
S
which is coherent with
\mathpzc{p}
. Either
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{m}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
then
\mathpzc{m}\in C_{\mathpzc{p}}
, or there exists a prefix
\mathpzc{m}_{0}\kappa^{-}
of
\mathpzc{m}
such that
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{m}_{0}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
and
\kappa^{-}
does not occur in
\mathpzc{p}
. In such a case,
\mathpzc{m}_{0}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in C_{\mathpzc{p}}
and either
\mathpzc{m}=\mathpzc{m}_{0}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
which belongs to
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
, or
\mathpzc{m}\not\coh\mathpzc{m}_{0}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
, i.e.,
\mathpzc{m}\not\coh C_{\mathpzc{p}}
.
Finally the path
\mathpzc{p}
has a finite length, hence a path in
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
has a length bounded by the length of
\mathpzc{p}
(no possibility of using twice an action by linearity condition). A path of
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
is either a path in
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
, hence its length is bounded by the length of
\mathpzc{p}
, or extended by a sequence of the form
\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
as
{\scriptstyle\maltese}
should end a path, thus its length is bounded by the length of
\mathpzc{p}
plus
2
.
Thus there cannot be infinite strictly increasing sequences in
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
.

iii)\Rightarrow i)
This result is obvious.

Let us now define the negative saturation condition.
The negative saturation condition ensures that, as soon as a path
\mathpzc{p}
belongs to
S
, and
\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}
generates a design which is orthogonal with all positively satured maximal cliques of
S
, then
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
.

{defi}

[Negative saturation condition]
Let
S
be a set of legal paths of same base, prefix-closed and daimon-closed.

S
satisfies
negative saturation
if for all path
\mathpzc{p}\in S
such that
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
is a legal path and for all positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
S
we have that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
,
then the path
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
.

The following lemma gives rise to equivalent formulations for the negative saturation condition.

Lemma 7
.

Let
S
be a set of legal paths of same base, prefix-closed and daimon-closed. Let
\mathpzc{p}
be a path belonging to
S
,
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
be a legal path. Then, the three following conditions are equivalent:

i)

For all positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
S
, we have
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
.

ii)

For all positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
S
without infinite strictly increasing sequence, we have
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
.

iii)

For all positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
S
, for all legal path
\mathpzc{m}
in the design
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
, for all negative action
\kappa_{0}^{-}
such that
\overline{\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}}
is a path in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
then
\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}
is a path of
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
.

Proof 3.3
.

i)\Rightarrow ii)
The result is obvious.

ii)\Rightarrow i)
Let
C
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
S
and suppose that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\not\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. As paths in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
have finite length, divergence occurs in a finite number of steps, say
n
. Because
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
has all negative actions, we know that the action that causes divergence is a positive one in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
, i.e., the dual negative action is not available in
C
.
Let us define a design
{\mathfrak{D}}
to be the set of chronicles
{\mathfrak{c}}\kappa^{\prime-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
as soon as
{\mathfrak{c}}
has length
n+1
and there exist actions
\kappa^{\prime-}
and
\kappa^{\prime+}
such that
{\mathfrak{c}}\kappa^{\prime-}\kappa^{\prime+}\in\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
. Let
C^{\prime}
be the set of paths
\mathpzc{q}
such that
\mathpzc{q}
is a path in
{\mathfrak{D}}
and either
\mathpzc{q}\in C
or
\mathpzc{q}=\mathpzc{q}_{0}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
and there exists a positive action
\kappa^{\prime\prime+}
such that
\mathpzc{q}_{0}\kappa^{\prime\prime+}\in C
. Remark that
C^{\prime}
is a clique as all paths are in a design, and that
C^{\prime}
is maximal and positively saturated as
C
is maximal and positively saturated. Hence by hypothesis
\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C^{\prime}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
:
\left<\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C^{\prime}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>=\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}\mathpzc{m}^{\prime}
. Hence contradiction as
\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}
should also be the prefix of a path in
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
.

iii)\Rightarrow i)
Let
C
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
S
. Suppose that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\not\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. Let
\mathpzc{m}
be the longest path in
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
such that
\overline{\mathpzc{m}}
is a path in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
(as
\mathpzc{p}
has a finite length, paths in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
have also a finite length, thus
\mathpzc{m}
is well defined). The path
\mathpzc{m}
is necessarily daimon-free otherwise the interaction converges. As
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
is complete with respect to negative action, there is a negative action
\kappa_{0}^{-}
such that
\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}
is not a path in
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
whereas
\overline{\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}}
is a path in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. In that case we should have in fact
\overline{\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}}
to be a path in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
. Thus
\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}
is a path in
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
(because of hypothesis
iii
). Contradiction. Thus
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
.

i)\Rightarrow iii)
Let
C
be a positive saturated maximal clique of
S
, let
\mathpzc{m}
be a legal path in the design
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
, let
\kappa_{0}^{-}
be a negative action such that
\overline{\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}}
is a path in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
. Then, since the interaction path between
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
and
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
begins with the path
\mathpzc{m}
, it should go on with
\overline{\kappa_{0}^{-}}
in
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
, then
\mathpzc{m}\kappa_{0}^{-}
is a path in
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
.

3.3.
Ludicable sets

We are now ready for fully characterizing a behaviour in terms of visitable paths:

•

The set of visitable paths of a behaviour is
ludicable
(proposition
8
).

•

A
ludicable
set of paths is the set of visitable paths of some behaviour (proposition
9
).

{defi}

[Ludicable set]
A set
S
of legal paths of same base is
pre-ludicable
when
S
is prefix-closed, daimon-closed, positively and negatively saturated.

A set
S
is
ludicable
if
S
and
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.70831pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}$}}}{\makebox[6.70831pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}$}}}{\makebox[5.29308pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}$}}}{\makebox[4.53476pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}$}}}}
are pre-ludicable.

Proposition 8
.

Let
{\mathbf{E}}
be a behaviour, then its set of visitable paths
V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
is ludicable.

Proof 3.4
.

We just need to check that
V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
is pre-ludicable: When
{\mathbf{E}}
is a behaviour we have
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[14.46666pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}$}}}{\makebox[14.46666pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}$}}}{\makebox[11.83325pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{775504}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{775504}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{775504}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{775504}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}$}}}{\makebox[10.91664pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{715433}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{715433}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{715433}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{715433}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}$}}}}=V_{{{\mathbf{E}}}^{\perp}}
, hence
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[14.46666pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}$}}}{\makebox[14.46666pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{948087}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}$}}}{\makebox[11.83325pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{775504}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{775504}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{775504}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{775504}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}$}}}{\makebox[10.91664pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{715433}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{715433}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{715433}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{715433}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}}}}$}}}}
is also pre-ludicable.

•

V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
is both daimon and positive prefix closed. This is a direct consequence of the following fact: When a design
{\mathfrak{D}}
is obtained from a design
{{\mathfrak{E}}}
by replacing chronicles
{\mathfrak{c}}\kappa^{+}{\mathfrak{c^{\prime}}}
of
{\mathfrak{E}}
by the chronicle
{\mathfrak{c}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
then
{{\mathfrak{E}}}^{\perp}\subset{{\mathfrak{D}}}^{\perp}
.

•

Positive saturation. Let
\mathpzc{p}
be a visitable path of
V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
. Then the design
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
belongs to
{\mathbf{E}}
. Let us consider the clique

C_{\mathpzc{p}}=\{\mathpzc{q}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \mathpzc{q}\in V_{{\mathbf{E}}},\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\}\cup\{\mathpzc{w}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \mathpzc{w}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{E}}},\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{w}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$},\raisebox{0.72041pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{w}\kappa^{-}}\raisebox{0.72041pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\not\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\}

We remark that
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
is a maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
. Furthermore the design
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{\mathpzc{p}}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
is the incarnation of
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
with respect to
{\mathbf{E}}
, hence
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{\mathpzc{p}}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
belongs to
{\mathbf{E}}
.

Let
\mathpzc{m}
and
\mathpzc{n}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}
be two paths belonging to
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
, and suppose that
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
, so
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{m\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\in{{\mathbf{E}}}^{\perp}
.
Note that the path
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}
should be a prefix of
\left<\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{\mathpzc{p}}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>
and that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{\mathpzc{p}}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. Hence there exists a positive action
\kappa^{+}
such that
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}
is a prefix of
\left<\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{\mathpzc{p}}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>
.
In other words,
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\in V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
.

Conclusion:
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
is positively saturated.

•

Negative saturation. Suppose that
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
is a legal path such that
\mathpzc{p}\in V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
and for all positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
we have that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
.
Let
{\mathfrak{D}}\in|{\mathbf{E}}|
, it follows from proposition
5
that there exists a positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
such that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}={\mathfrak{D}}
, therefore
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\perp{\mathfrak{D}}
. Thus
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\in{\mathbf{E}}^{\perp}
. Finally
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\in{\mathbf{E}}
and
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}=\left<\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>
, thus
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
.
∎

Our issue now is to prove that if a set
S
of paths is ludicable then it is the set of visitable paths of some behaviour
{\mathbf{A}}
.
Previously, it is important to notice that such a behaviour
{\mathbf{A}}
may not be unique. In some cases, in particular when
S
is finite, the incarnation of
{\mathbf{A}}
is exactly defined from maximal cliques of
S
, hence
{\mathbf{A}}
is unique. However, when
S
is infinite and, more precisely when it contains at least one infinite strictly increasing sequence of paths, several choices of behaviour are possible.

{exa}

Let us consider for example a set
S
generated by an infinite strictly increasing sequence
{\mathfrak{c}}_{0}=\kappa_{0}^{+}
and
{\mathfrak{c}}_{i}={\mathfrak{c}}_{i-1}\kappa_{i}^{-}\kappa_{i}^{+}
, for
i\geq 1
, where each action except
\kappa_{0}^{+}
is justified by the previous one:
\kappa_{i}^{+}
is justified by
\kappa_{i}^{-}
and
\kappa_{i+1}^{-}
is justified by
\kappa_{i}^{+}
. Formally,

S=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}\cup\{{\mathfrak{c}}_{i}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ i\geq 0\}\cup\{{\mathfrak{c}}_{i-1}\kappa_{i}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ i\geq 1\}

Note that the elements of
S
are in fact chronicles.
Let us consider the two following behaviours:

\begin{array}[]{rcl}{\mathbf{A}}_{1}&=&\{\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ C\mbox{ is a maximal clique of }S\}^{\perp\perp}\\
{\mathbf{A}}_{2}&=&\{\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{D}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ D\mbox{ is a maximal clique of }\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.70831pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}$}}}{\makebox[6.70831pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}$}}}{\makebox[5.29308pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}$}}}{\makebox[4.53476pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}$}}}}\}^{\perp}\end{array}

It is worth noticing that
S
is ludicable and that
S=V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{1}}=V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{2}}
, although
{\mathbf{A}}_{1}\neq{\mathbf{A}}_{2}
.
The difference between
{\mathbf{A}}_{1}
and
{\mathbf{A}}_{2}
is that
\bigcup_{i}{\mathfrak{c}}_{i}
is a design of
{\mathbf{A}}_{1}
but not of
{\mathbf{A}}_{2}
. Whereas
{\mathbf{A}}_{2}
contains only designs generated by bounded maximal cliques of
S
of the form
\{{\mathfrak{c}}_{i}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ i\leq N\}\cup\{{\mathfrak{c}}_{N}\kappa_{N}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}
. On the opposite,
\bigcup_{i}\overline{{\mathfrak{c}}_{i}}
belongs to
{{\mathbf{A}}_{2}}^{\perp}
.

Proposition 9
.

Let
S
be a non-empty set of legal paths of same base, if
S
is ludicable then there exists a behaviour
{\mathbf{E}}
such that
S=V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
.

Proof 3.5
.

We set:

-
E=\{\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ C
is a positively saturated maximal clique of
S\}
,

-
F=\{\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{D}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ D
is a positively saturated maximal clique of
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.70831pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}$}}}{\makebox[6.70831pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}$}}}{\makebox[5.29308pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}$}}}{\makebox[4.53476pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}$}}}}
with no infinite strictly increasing sequences of paths
\}
.

We shall prove that
S=V_{F^{\perp}}
. There may be different choices for
E
and
F
with the same result as it may be deduced from example
3.4
: for each infinite strictly increasing sequence of
S
, either
E
or
F
should have a restriction.

Note that with conditions as stated on
E
and
F
, normalization between a design of
E
and a design of
F
cannot continue infinitely: either it converges or it stops because a positive action in one side has no negative counterpart on the other side.

The proof sketch is as follows:

i)

We prove first that
E\subset F^{\perp}
(hence
F\subset F^{\perp\perp}\subset E^{\perp}
).

ii)

Next we prove that
S\subset V_{F^{\perp}}
.

iii)

Then, we prove that
V_{F^{\perp}}\subset S
.

iv)

We conclude from ii) and iii) that
S=V_{F^{\perp}}
and the fact that
F^{\perp}
is a behaviour.

i) We prove that
E\subset{F}^{\perp}
.
We will show that the interaction between a design of
E
and a design of
F
does not diverge. Therefore, since by construction the interaction cannot go on infinitely, it converges, so
E\subset{F}^{\perp}
.
Namely, let
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\in E
and
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{D}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\in F
, we show by induction on the length of
\mathpzc{p}
, a strict prefix of the interaction path of
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
with
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{D}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
, that:

either
\mathpzc{p}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in C
, or
\overline{\mathpzc{p}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in D
, or there exists a proper action
\kappa
such that
\mathpzc{p\kappa}
is a prefix of a path of
C
and
\overline{\mathpzc{p\kappa}}
is a prefix of a path of
D
.

It follows not only that the interaction path continues but it remains a prefix of an element of
S
as
\mathpzc{p}
(resp.
\overline{\mathpzc{p}}
) is a prefix of an element of
C
(resp. of
D
).

\mathpzc{p}\kappa\in S
, against the hypothesis that

is the longest prefix of

that is a prefix of an element of

We conclude from ii) and iii) that

and the fact that

is a behaviour.

3.4.
Ludicable closures

In the previous subsection, propositions
8
and
9
give necessary and sufficient conditions for relating sets of paths and behaviours. In this subsection we give a constructive means for closing a set of paths
S
, i.e., for obtaining the minimal ludicable set containing
S
.

{defi}

[Ludicable Closure]
Let
S
be a set of legal paths of the same base, we define the pre-ludicable closure, written
S^{\prime}
, of
S
to be the smallest set of paths including
S
that is prefix-closed, daimon-closed, and that satisfies negative saturation and positive saturation.

The
ludicable closure
of
S
, written
LC(S)
, is
\bigcup_{n}S_{n}
such that the family
(S_{n})
is defined inductively in the following way:

•

S_{0}=S
.

•

S_{n+1}=S_{n}\cup S_{n}^{\prime}\cup\makebox[22.735pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{6.76599pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.76599pt}{$\resizebox{1489961}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{({\makebox[12.15164pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{6.14993pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}$}}})^{\prime}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.76599pt}{$\resizebox{1489961}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{({\makebox[12.15164pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{6.14993pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}$}}})^{\prime}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.76599pt}{$\resizebox{1489961}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{({\makebox[12.15164pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{6.14993pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{6.14993pt}{$\resizebox{796370}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S_{n}}}{\hbox Lemma 12
.

Let
E
be a set of designs of same base, let
C
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
LC(V_{E})
such that if there is an infinite increasing sequence of paths
(\mathpzc{p}_{i})
in
C
then
\bigcup\mathpzc{p}_{i}
is already a path in a design of
E
, then
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\in E^{\perp\perp}
.

Proof 3.8
.

Let
{\mathfrak{D}}\in|E^{\perp}|
.

(1)

The interaction path between
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
and the design
{\mathfrak{D}}
cannot be infinite:
For each infinite increasing sequence of paths
(\mathpzc{p}_{i})
in
C
, the path
\bigcup\mathpzc{p}_{i}
is already included in a design of
E
, hence there is an index
i_{0}
such that
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p_{i_{0}}}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset{\mathfrak{D}}
.

4.
A Characterization of MALL behaviours

This section is devoted to a characterization of MALL behaviours in terms of their visitable paths. A MALL behaviour is built from constants
\bf 1
,
\bf 0
,
\mathord{\mathchoice{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}}{\mkern 4.0mu\raise-0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\raise 0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern 2.0mu}{\mkern 4.0mu\raise-0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\raise 0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern 2.0mu}}
,
\mathord{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\bot$}\mkern-13.5mu\hbox{$\bot$}\mkern-13.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\bot$}}
and connectives multiplicative tensor ‘
\otimes
’, additive sum ‘
\oplus
’, shift ‘
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shpos$}}}}
’ and their duals. We first recall definitions and properties of these connectives. We give an example showing that there exist behaviours that are not the denotation of a MALL behaviour. We prove then that a MALL behaviour satisfies two criteria: finiteness, i.e., the incarnation has a finite number of designs and these designs are finite, and regularity, i.e., a legal path built from actions in designs of the incarnation should be visitable.

4.1.
Linear Connectives

Before establishing properties concerning the behaviours which may be associated with linear formulas,
we recall below the main linear operations on behaviours: multiplicative tensor ‘
\otimes
’, additive sum ‘
\oplus
’ and also the shift ‘
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shpos$}}}}
’ operation. The shift operation is required as the logic is polarized: it allows for switching from/to a positive behaviour to/from a negative behaviour. Dual operations are defined in a standard way:
{\mathbf{A}}\invamp{\mathbf{B}}=({\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}})^{\perp}
,
{\mathbf{A}}\with{\mathbf{B}}=({\mathbf{A}}\oplus{\mathbf{B}})^{\perp}
and
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shneg$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shneg$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shneg$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shneg$}}}}{\mathbf{A}}=(\mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shpos$}}}}{\mathbf{A}})^{\perp}
.

for
\bf 1
):

{defi}

\bf 1=\{\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\},(+,\xi,\emptyset)\}
,

\mathord{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\bot$}\mkern-13.5mu\hbox{$\bot$}\mkern-13.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\bot$}}=\bf 1^{\perp}
,

\bf 0=\{\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}\}
,

\mathord{\mathchoice{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}}{\mkern 4.0mu\raise-0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\raise 0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern 2.0mu}{\mkern 4.0mu\raise-0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\raise 0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern 2.0mu}}=\bf 0^{\perp}
.

We intend to relate MALL logical connectives, in fact ‘
\otimes
’, ‘
\oplus
’, ‘
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shpos$}}}}
’, with operations on visitable paths. Obtaining the set of visitable paths for ‘
\oplus
’ and ‘
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shpos$}}}}
’ is quite immediate. The behaviour
{\mathbf{A}}\oplus{\mathbf{B}}
is the union of the two behaviours
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
, hence visitable paths of the result should be the union of the two sets of visitable paths.
The behaviour
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shpos$}}}}{\mathbf{A}}
is built by adding to each design the same action at the root, hence visitable paths of the resulting behaviour should be built by adding this action as prefix of visitable paths of
{\mathbf{A}}
. As the operation ‘
\otimes
’ models a kind of concurrency, it is natural to consider that the set of visitable paths of a tensor should be in some way the shuffle of the sets of visitable paths. Without surprise, it is necessary to consider only legal paths among the ones obtained by shuffle of visitable paths.
However, being a legal path in the shuffle is not sufficient as shown in example
4.1
.

{exa}

Let us consider the two behaviours
{\mathbf{A}}
which incarnation is the daimon-closure of the set
\{{\mathfrak{A}}_{1},{\mathfrak{A}}_{2}\}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
which incarnation is the daimon-closure of the set
\{{\mathfrak{B}}_{1},{\mathfrak{B}}_{2}\}
:

In example
4.1
, the behaviour
{\mathbf{B}}
is not decomposable by means of linear connectives. We present in the following section a very simple characterization of behaviours which may be recursively decomposable by means of linear connectives. For such an issue we introduce the notion of regular behaviour.

4.2.
Regular Behaviours

We prove in this subsection that finiteness and regularity as defined later characterize a behaviour for being the denotation of a MALL formula.

{defi}

[Trivial view/chronicle]
A legal path which is equal to its view is a chronicle. When a chronicle (view)
{\mathfrak{c}}
is such that
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.44444pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.44444pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{291271}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{291271}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{291271}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{291271}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{{\mathfrak{c}}}}$}}}{\makebox[4.44444pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.44444pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{291271}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{291271}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{291271}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{291271}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{{\mathfrak{c}}}}$}}}{\makebox[3.55557pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.41112pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{233018}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{233018}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{233018}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{233018}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle{\mathfrak{c}}}}$}}}{\makebox[3.05559pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{1.72221pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{200251}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{200251}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{200251}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{c}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{200251}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle{\mathfrak{c}}}}$}}}}
is also a chronicle, or, in other words, each action of
{\mathfrak{c}}
is justified by the immediate previous one, except the first one which is initial, this chronicle is said to be
trivial
.

If
w\kappa w^{\prime}
is a path with
\kappa
a proper action, the
trivial chronicle of
\kappa
for
w\kappa w^{\prime}
is a trivial chronicle with last action
\kappa
that is a subsequence of
w\kappa
.

Note that an action occurs only once in a path hence there is only one trivial chronicle of a given proper action that is a subsequence of this path.

In the following we consider mainly legal paths. For that purpose we introduce a specific definition.

{defi}

[Shuffle of two sets of legal paths]
Let
V
and

Let us consider first that

•

•

\mathpzc{p}=\mathpzc{c}\kappa\mathpzc{d}
where

is a trivial chronicle.

– Or
\kappa
is justified by an action
\kappa_{0}
, and we may write
\mathpzc{p}=\mathpzc{c}_{0}\kappa_{0}\mathpzc{c}_{1}\kappa\mathpzc{d}
, where
\mathpzc{c}_{0}\kappa_{0}\mathpzc{c}_{1}
and
\mathpzc{c}_{0}\kappa_{0}\kappa\mathpzc{d}
are two chronicles having at most

positive actions which are not justified by their immediate previous negative action. That
\mathpzc{c}_{0}\kappa_{0}\kappa\mathpzc{d}
is indeed a chronicle is due to the fact that in

all actions are immediately justifed by the immediate previous one. Then, by induction hypothesis,

\mathpzc{p}

V

\mathpzc{p}\in V

\mathpzc{p}
is a chronicle we know already that
\mathpzc{p}\in V

•

V

n

; furthermore

is a legal path hence, by induction hypothesis,

.

– Or
\kappa
is justified by an action

, and we may write

is a legal path,

could not be a path,

and

.

That a data

contains all legal paths written from a set of justified actions is not only a necessary condition to be regular, but it is also sufficient as stated in the following proposition.

Proposition 17
.

Let
V
be a set of legal paths of base
\beta
such that
V/\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.05556pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}$}}}{\makebox[8.05556pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}$}}}{\makebox[6.44447pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}$}}}{\makebox[5.52786pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}$}}}}
is non-additive.

is a regular data.

Proof 4.3
.

Note that, if
V
is complete,
V
is exactly the set of legal paths of base
\beta
which may be written from actions in paths of
V
.
Let
\mathpzc{p}\in V
then prefixes and views of
\mathpzc{p}
are made of actions of
\mathpzc{p}
hence are elements of
V
as
V
is complete.
Similarly, let
\mathpzc{p},\mathpzc{q}\in V
then shuffles of
\mathpzc{p}
and
\mathpzc{q}
are made of actions of paths of
V
hence are elements of
V
.
The same applies for
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.05556pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}$}}}{\makebox[8.05556pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}$}}}{\makebox[6.44447pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}$}}}{\makebox[5.52786pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}$}}}}
.
Finally, as

is prefix-closed,
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[8.05556pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}$}}}{\makebox[8.05556pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{527929}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V}}$}}}{\makebox[6.44447pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{422345}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V}}$}}}{\makebox[5.52786pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{362274}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V}}$}}}}
is daimon-closed, and vice-versa.

Let us go back now to the general case where the data

may be additive. The following proposition links properties of the non-additive case to the general case.

Proof 4.4
.

are shuffle closed.

Proposition 19
.

Let

be a set of legal paths. If

Let
\mathpzc{v}
(resp.
\mathpzc{s}
) be the subsequence of
\mathpzc{r}
made of actions of
V
(resp.
S
), hence with foci subaddresses of
\sigma
(resp.
\tau
).
Note that if
\mathpzc{r}=w_{1}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}w_{2}
then
\kappa^{-}
and
\kappa^{+}
are subaddresses either the two of
\sigma
or the two of
\tau
for
\mathpzc{r}
to be a path.
Thus
\mathpzc{v}
(resp.
\mathpzc{s}
) is a finite alternated sequence of actions based on
\sigma\vdash
(resp.
\tau\vdash
). As actions of
\mathpzc{r}
have distinct foci and, if the daimon is present, it is its last action, this is also the case for
\mathpzc{v}
and
\mathpzc{s}
.
Furthermore, let
\kappa^{+}
be an action of
\mathpzc{v}
justified by
\kappa^{-}
in
\mathpzc{r}
, let
\mathpzc{r}=r_{0}\kappa^{-}r_{1}\kappa^{+}r_{2}
and
\mathpzc{v}=v_{1}\kappa v_{2}
, then
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner$}{r_{0}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\urcorner$}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}=\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\ulcorner$}{r_{0}\kappa^{-}r_{1}\kappa^{+}}\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\urcorner$}=\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\ulcorner$}{v_{1}\kappa^{+}}\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\urcorner$}
thus
\mathpzc{v}
is a path. Similarly
\mathpzc{s}
is a path.
Finally, with lemma
34
(see annex
4.2
), we have that
\mathpzc{v}
and
\mathpzc{s}
are legal paths.

\mathpzc{v}\in V
and
\mathpzc{s}\in S

Proposition 21
.

Let
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
be two positive alien behaviours distinct from
{\mathbf{0}}
and based on
\vdash\xi
,
{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}
is regular iff
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
are regular.

Proof 4.7
.

We just consider the paradigmatic case: as
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
are distinct from
\bf 0
, we can suppose that designs of
{\mathbf{A}}
distinct from
{\scriptstyle\maltese}
have as first action
(+,\xi,I)
and designs of
{\mathbf{B}}
distinct from
{\scriptstyle\maltese}
have as first action
(+,\xi,J)
and
I\cap J=\emptyset
.

•

Let
{\mathbf{A}}
and

22
is a joint work with A. Pavaux. One may find in

]
the proof in a framework of Ludics à la Terui. A. Pavaux proposed also in

Pav17
]
a different proof of proposition
21
based on proposition
22
. In her paper, she uses these results for studying a representation of data and function types.

Proof 4.8
.

See annex
A.2
.

We are now able to state the main theorem of this section: MALL formulas are denoted by regular and finite behaviours. A behaviour is finite when it contains only a finite number of designs in the incarnation and these designs are finite, i.e., each such design has a finite number of actions.

Theorem 23
.

Let
{\mathbf{E}}
be a behaviour.
{\mathbf{E}}
is regular and finite iff it is generated by the following grammar:

\displaystyle{\mathbf{P}}

\displaystyle::=\bf 0\penalty\ |\penalty\ \bf 1\penalty\ |\penalty\ \mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shpos$}}}}{\mathbf{N}}\penalty\ |\penalty\ {{\mathbf{N}}}^{\perp}\penalty\ |\penalty\ {\mathbf{P}}\otimes{\mathbf{P}}\penalty\ |\penalty\ {\mathbf{P}}\oplus{\mathbf{P}}

\displaystyle{\mathbf{N}}

\displaystyle::=\mathord{\mathchoice{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}}{\mkern 4.0mu\raise-0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\raise 0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern 2.0mu}{\mkern 4.0mu\raise-0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\raise 0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern 2.0mu}}\penalty\ |\penalty\ \mathord{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\bot$}\mkern-13.5mu\hbox{$\bot$}\mkern-13.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\bot$}}\penalty\ |\penalty\ \mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shneg$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shneg$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shneg$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shneg$}}}}{\mathbf{P}}\penalty\ |\penalty\ {{\mathbf{P}}}^{\perp}\penalty\ |\penalty\ {\mathbf{N}}\invamp{\mathbf{N}}\penalty\ |\penalty\ {\mathbf{N}}\with{\mathbf{N}}

Proof 4.9
.

Let
{\mathbf{E}}
be a regular and finite behaviour, hence the proof may be done by induction on the number of distinct actions present in designs in the incarnation. The main ingredients are the following. If
{\mathbf{E}}
has a negative base, consider its dual
{\mathbf{E}}^{\perp}
, thus of positive base, that has the same number of distinct actions.
If
{\mathbf{E}}
is different from
\bf 0
and
\bf 1
then
{\mathbf{E}}
may be decomposed as a
\oplus
of connected behaviours
{\mathbf{E}}_{i}
, one for each distinct first action
[
Gir01
]
.
Obviously each
{\mathbf{E}}_{i}
is a finite behaviour.
Remark that the family
(V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}/\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[17.6345pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{1155695}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{1155695}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{1155695}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{1155695}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}$}}}{\makebox[17.6345pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{1155695}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{1155695}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{1155695}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{1155695}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}$}}}{\makebox[15.0011pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{983112}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{983112}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{983112}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{983112}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}$}}}{\makebox[14.08449pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{923041}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{923041}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{923041}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{923041}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}}}$}}}})
is the family of maximal non-additive data such that
V_{{\mathbf{E}}_{i}}\subset V_{{\mathbf{E}}}
.
Thus
{\mathbf{E}}_{i}
is a regular behaviour (consequence of Lemma
18
).
A connected, regular and finite behaviour may be decomposed as a tensor of regular and finite behaviours (Proposition
21
), or a shift when the first ramification has only one element.
Conversely,
it is immediate that
\bf 0
and
\bf 1
are regular and regularity is stable by connectives
\cdot^{\perp}
and
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\displaystyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.9pt\hbox{\scalebox{1.1}{$\textstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptstyle\shpos$}}}{\raise 0.1pt\hbox{\scalebox{1}{$\scriptscriptstyle\shpos$}}}}
. Finally it follows from Lemma
18
and Proposition
21
that regularity is also stable by
\oplus
and
\otimes
.

Note that theorem
23
is a full characterization of MALL behaviours amongst finite behaviours: there exist finite behaviours that are not regular, hence not generated by the previous grammar.

{\mathbf{B}}

}

{\mathfrak{C}}_{2}=\!\!\!\!\!\!\scalebox{.8}{
\hbox{\vbox{\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\halign{\relax\global\@RightOffset=0pt \@ReturnLeftOffsettrue$\inferstyle#$&&
\inferTabSkip\global\@RightOffset=0pt \@ReturnLeftOffsetfalse$\inferstyle#$\cr\textstyle$\hbox{\vbox{\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\halign{\relax\global\@RightOffset=0pt \@ReturnLeftOffsettrue$\inferstyle#$&&
\inferTabSkip\global\@RightOffset=0pt \@ReturnLeftOffsetfalse$\inferstyle#$\cr\textstyle$\hbox{\vbox{\moveright 16.1614pt\vbox{\halign{\relax\global\@RightOffset=0pt \@ReturnLeftOffsettrue$\inferstyle#$&&
\inferTabSkip\global\@RightOffset=0pt \@ReturnLeftOffsetfalse$\inferstyle#$\cr\textstyle\cr}}\kern 2.0pt\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule width=32.32283pt}\kern 2.0pt\moveright 0.0pt\hbox{$\textstyle\vdash\beta 011$}}\kern-312.67717pt\kern 5.0pt\raise 6.53334pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\scriptstyle\maltese}$}\kern 300.9966pt}$\cr}}\kern 2.0pt\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule width=32.32283pt}\kern 2.0pt\moveright 3.88885pt\hbox{$\textstyle\beta 01\vdash$}}\kern-312.67717pt\kern 5.0pt\raise 6.22223pt\hbox{$\textstyle\lambda_{1}^{-}$}\kern 297.35768pt}$&\hskip 10.22217pt$\textstyle\beta 02\vdash\cr}}\kern 2.0pt\moveright 3.88885pt\vbox{\hrule width=386.1979pt}\kern 2.0pt\moveright 185.82642pt\hbox{$\textstyle\vdash\beta 0$}}\kern 45.08676pt\kern 5.0pt\raise 5.71332pt\hbox{$\textstyle\lambda_{0}^{+}$}\kern 0.0pt}
}

The behaviour
{\mathbf{C}}
is not regular. By the way, as the first proper action is unique and positive but not a shift, if
{\mathbf{C}}
were regular,
{\mathbf{C}}
should be a tensor of behaviours. But the tensor is commutative. In terms of interaction paths, this means that the path
\lambda_{0}^{+}\lambda_{1}^{-}\lambda_{1}^{+}\lambda_{2}^{-}\lambda_{2}^{+}
(left then right chronicle in
{\mathfrak{C}}_{1}
) is visitable iff the path
\lambda_{0}^{+}\lambda_{2}^{-}\lambda_{2}^{+}\lambda_{1}^{-}\lambda_{1}^{+}
(right then left chronicle in
{\mathfrak{C}}_{1}
) is visitable. However the first path is visitable but not the second one. In other words, interaction has to visit the left chronicle of
{\mathfrak{C}}_{1}
before the right one: non-commutativity is present there. Next section is devoted to understand in which extent non-commutative tensors may be considered in this framework.

Non-commutativity is not the only kind of non-regularity that we may observe as shown in example
4.7
.

{exa}

Let us consider the behaviour
{\mathbf{D}}=\{{\mathfrak{D}}_{1},{\mathfrak{D}}_{2}\}^{\perp\perp}
where designs
{\mathfrak{D}}_{1}
and
{\mathfrak{D}}_{2}
are given below.

{\mathfrak{D}}_{1}=\scalebox{.75}{

}
