{\mathbf{D}}
is a finite behaviour whose incarnation is the daimon-closure of these two designs, and
{\mathbf{D}}
is not regular. It cannot also be interpreted in terms of non-commutativity. Indeed, during an interaction, action
\alpha_{1}
may be followed by action
\beta_{1}
(or the converse), but not by action
\beta_{2}
(or
\alpha_{2}
). And this situation is symmetric changing indices
1
and
2
in the previous statement. This situation is a kind of entanglement as part of a (standard) tensor.
We let the study of such a situation to further works.

5.
Beyond Regular Behaviours

In previous sections we presented examples of behaviours that are not regular, hence are not generated by the connectives of multiplicative-additive Linear Logic. We propose in this section a study of non-commutative connectives, as they are defined in the literature, plus a new one.

Non-commutativity has been a subject of interest in Logic. J. Lambek
[
Lam58
]
developed an intuitionistic non-commutative logic by omitting the exchange rule of the sequent calculus but giving rise to two symbols of implication. With regards to Linear Logic, D. Yetter
[
Yet90
]
(after a talk given by J.-Y. Girard in 1987) studied a cyclic version: the exchange rule is replaced by a cyclic one over the list of formulas of a sequent. P. Ruet
[
Rue00
]
, with further works with M. Abrusci
[
AR99
]
and R. Maieli
[
MR03
]
, developed a logic fully integrating commutativity and non-commutativity. Again, this is the exchange rule that is replaced. In all these cases, non-commutativity arises spatially: the structure over the set/list of formulas in a sequent is non-commutative, however the choice of formula to be decomposed (in a bottom-up reading of proofs) does not depend on this structure.
In the following, we begin with the study of a non-commutative tensor
\olessthan
due to J.-Y. Girard
[
Gir01
]
but stable by regularity, hence adding it to MALL connectives does not extend the set of behaviours. This connective is not spatial but prioritize between operands when a choice between actions has to be done: only one action is kept. Then we study connectives that deal with temporality: what is at stake is to begin interaction with one operand before the other. This is the case with the sequoid
\oslash
connective proposed by M. Churchill, J. Laird and G. McCusker
[
CLM13
]
. Regularity is not stable by this connective as well as a new one we propose in a last subsection.

5.1.
A not so significant non-commutative connective.

If J.-Y. Girard presented non-commutative connectives in his seminal paper of Ludics
[
Gir01
]
, these are of no help for decomposing a behaviour. It is the case for the non-commutative tensor product
\olessthan
.
Let
{\mathfrak{A}}
and
{\mathfrak{B}}
be two designs, in
{\mathfrak{A}}\olessthan{\mathfrak{B}}
priority is given to chronicles of
{\mathfrak{B}}
when a choice has to be done. In terms of execution, i.e., visitable paths, priority is given to the strategy
{\mathfrak{B}}
again the strategy of
{\mathfrak{A}}
.
The connective
\olessthan
is defined when behaviours are not disjoint, i.e., the ramification of their first actions is not necessarily disjoint:

{defi}

Let
{\mathfrak{A}}
and
{\mathfrak{B}}
be two positive designs of same base
\vdash\xi
,

•

If
{\mathfrak{A}}=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}
or
{\mathfrak{B}}=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}
,
{\mathfrak{A}}\olessthan{\mathfrak{B}}={\mathfrak{A}}\otimes{\mathfrak{B}}=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}
.

•

Otherwise let
{\mathfrak{A}}=(+,\xi,I)(\bigcup_{j\in J,K_{j}}(-,\xi.j,K_{j}){\mathfrak{A}}_{j,K_{j}}\cup\bigcup_{i\not\in J,L_{i}}(-,\xi.i,L_{i}){\mathfrak{A}}_{i,L_{i}})
and
{\mathfrak{B}}=(+,\xi,J){\mathfrak{B}}^{\prime}
, then
{\mathfrak{A}}\olessthan{\mathfrak{B}}={\mathfrak{B}}\otimes(+,\xi,I\setminus J)\bigcup_{i\not\in J,L_{i}}(-,\xi.i,L_{i}){\mathfrak{A}}_{i,L_{i}}
.

Let
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
be two behaviours,
{\mathbf{A}}\olessthan{\mathbf{B}}=\{{\mathfrak{A}}\olessthan{\mathfrak{B}}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ {\mathfrak{A}}\in{\mathbf{A}},{\mathfrak{B}}\in{\mathbf{B}}\}^{\perp\perp}
.

The tensor
\olessthan
is non-commutative, however, as it immediately follows from the definition, the design
{\mathfrak{A}}\olessthan{\mathfrak{B}}
may always be viewed as the tensor of two designs.
As the connective
\olessthan
distributes over
\oplus

[
Gir01
]
, we can study this connective
\olessthan
on connected behaviours, i.e., behaviours with a unique first ramification: in this case in particular internal completeness is satisfied.
We remark in the following lemma a property that relates the non-commutative tensor of two behaviours with a commutative tensor of two behaviours.
Hence augmenting the grammar for regular behaviours with such a non-commutative tensor does not change the language of behaviours.

Lemma 24
.

Let
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
be two connected positive behaviours of base
\vdash\xi
, let
J
be such that
{\mathbf{B}}=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}\cup(+,\xi,J){\mathbf{B}}^{\prime}
. We consider the following function
\phi
: let
{\mathfrak{A}}\in{\mathbf{A}}
,

\phi({\mathfrak{A}})={\mathfrak{A}}\backslash\bigcup_{i\in I\cap J,K_{i}}(+,\xi,I)(-,\xi.i,K_{i}){\mathfrak{A}}_{i,K_{i}}

Let
\phi({\mathbf{A}})=\{\phi({\mathfrak{A}})\penalty\ ;\penalty\ {\mathfrak{A}}\in{\mathbf{A}}\}
.
Then
{\mathbf{A}}\olessthan{\mathbf{B}}=\phi({\mathbf{A}})^{\perp\perp}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}
.

Proof 5.1
.

Note that
\phi({\mathfrak{A}})
is always a design hence
\phi({\mathbf{A}})^{\perp\perp}
is a behaviour.
Remark first that, as behaviours are connected, for designs
{\mathfrak{A}}\in{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathfrak{B}}\in{\mathbf{B}}
, we have that
{\mathfrak{A}}\olessthan{\mathfrak{B}}=\phi({\mathfrak{A}})\otimes{\mathfrak{B}}
.

Hence
{\mathbf{A}}\olessthan{\mathbf{B}}=(\phi({\mathbf{A}})\otimes{\mathbf{B}})^{\perp\perp}=(\phi({\mathbf{A}})^{\perp\perp}\otimes{\mathbf{B}})^{\perp\perp}=\phi({\mathbf{A}})^{\perp\perp}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}
.

5.2.
The sequoid
\oslash
game
[
CLM13
]

M. Churchill, J. Laird and G. McCusker proposed in
[
CLM13
]
a first-order logic
WS1
and a games model in which proofs denote history-sensitive strategies. We do not consider here the full logic but only represent in terms of Ludics the essence of their main specific non-commutative tensor connective
\oslash
. Briefly speaking, the first move in a play of
{\mathbf{A}}\oslash{\mathbf{B}}
has to be done in
{\mathbf{A}}
, the following moves are considered as with the standard commutative tensor. We show how such a connective may be defined in our setting by considering an adequate set of visitable paths. Obviously such a set of visitable paths should contain
{\scriptstyle\maltese}
and the first (positive) action of
{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}
. Furthermore, it should contain visitable paths of
{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}
with the restriction that the second action “comes” from
{\mathbf{A}}
.

Proposition 25
.

Let
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
be two connected disjoint positive behaviours of base
\vdash\xi
,
let
\kappa_{0}^{+}
(resp.
\kappa_{{\mathbf{A}}}^{+}
) be the first action of designs in
{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}
(resp.
{\mathbf{A}}
),
let
S=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese},\kappa_{0}^{+}\}\cup\{\kappa_{0}^{+}\kappa_{0}^{-}\mathpzc{s}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \kappa_{{\mathbf{A}}}^{+}\kappa_{0}^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}},\kappa_{0}^{+}\kappa_{0}^{-}\mathpzc{s}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}}\}
.
Then
S
is ludicable.

Proof 5.2
.

S
is a set of legal paths as a subset of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}}
.

S
is also daimon and prefix closed.

S
is pre-ludicable:

•

Positive saturation: let
\mathpzc{p}\in S
, let us consider the set
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
for
S
. Let
\mathpzc{m}\in C_{\mathpzc{p}}
,
\mathpzc{n}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\in C_{\mathpzc{p}}
,
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
, note that
C_{\mathpzc{p}}\subset D_{\mathpzc{p}}
where
D_{\mathpzc{p}}
is the positively saturated maximal clique for
\mathpzc{p}
in
V_{{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}}
. Thus
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\in D_{\mathpzc{p}}
. Hence
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}\in C_{\mathpzc{p}}
as
\mathpzc{m}\kappa^{-}\kappa^{+}
satisfies the required properties for being in
S
. Thus
C_{\mathpzc{p}}
is positively saturated.

•

Negative saturation: let
\mathpzc{p}\in S
,
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
be a legal path, suppose that for all positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
S
,
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
, then for all positively saturated maximal clique
D
of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}}
, we have also that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{D}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
, then
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}}
. Thus
\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
as conditions are fulfilled.

\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.70831pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}$}}}{\makebox[6.70831pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{5.46666pt}{$\resizebox{439636}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{S}}$}}}{\makebox[5.29308pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.82668pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.82668pt}{$\resizebox{346887}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle S}}$}}}{\makebox[4.53476pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.73334pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.73334pt}{$\resizebox{297190}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle S}}$}}}}
is pre-ludicable: The proof is similar noticing that
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[27.97916pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{5.46666pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox is pre-ludicable.

It is straightforward to notice that

as defined before is the set of visitable paths of a behaviour
{\mathbf{A}}\oslash{\mathbf{B}}
with properties as required in the logic

[

]
. We do not go further on the study of
WS1
in our framework, we just remark the strength of our approach to prove that a connective is well-defined when given in terms of visitable paths (or plays). Note finally that
{\mathbf{A}}\oslash{\mathbf{B}}
is not a regular behaviour hence this connective may really augment the grammar of MALL.

5.3.

When
\mathpzc{q}
is not empty, the path
\mathpzc{p}
should be maximal with respect to the design
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
it generates, otherwise it could be possible to switch back from
\mathpzc{q}
to a path in
{\mathbf{A}}
, what should be rejected.
Note that if a visitable path is maximal with respect to its generated design then it is also maximal with respect to length. The converse is not always true as stated in example
5.3
.

Proposition 26
.

Let
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
be two connected disjoint positive behaviours of base
\vdash\xi
, let us consider the three following definitions:

•

V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
is the set of paths
\kappa w
of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}\otimes{\mathbf{B}}}
such that
w
contains only actions of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}}
.

•

V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}=\{\mathpzc{p}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \mathpzc{p}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}},\mathpzc{p}\penalty\ {\scriptstyle\maltese}
-free,
\nexists\mathpzc{q}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}},\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subsetneq\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\}

•

V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}=\{\mathpzc{q}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \exists\kappa^{+},\kappa^{+}\mathpzc{q}\in V_{{\mathbf{B}}}\}

Suppose moreover that the behaviour
{\mathbf{A}}
satisfies the following constraint
(C)
:

(C)
For each
\mathpzc{p}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}}
and
\mathpzc{q}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}}^{max}
such that
\mathpzc{p}
and
\mathpzc{q}
end on the same (positive) action and
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{q}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
, then
\mathpzc{p}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}}^{max}
.

Then
S=V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}\cup V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
is ludicable.

Remark that
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}
is the subset of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
such that paths generate designs that have no extension in the incarnation
|{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}|
of
{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}
: such paths are maximal with respect to designs they generate in
|{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}|
.
Remark also that
V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
is obtained by deleting the first action of a path of
V_{{\mathbf{B}}}
: this first action is already ‘taken into account’ by the first action of paths of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
.
Example
5.3
proposes such a construction.
Example
5.3
shows that constraint
(C)
is required otherwise unexpected visitable paths appear. However there is always a possibility to define the ludicable closure of
S
(see
subsection
3.4
). Thus the connective

Lemma 27
.

S

Proof 5.3
.

Paths of

are legal and paths of

differ from paths of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}}
only because of the ramification of the first (hence positive) action that is a larger set.

Let
\mathpzc{p}\mathpzc{q}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
(with conventions of notation given above).
\mathpzc{p}
is legal as
\mathpzc{p}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
.
Note that an action in
\mathpzc{q}
is necessarily justified by the first action of
\mathpzc{p}
: the base contains a unique positive address, and behaviours
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
are connected and disjoint.
Let
\mathpzc{p}\mathpzc{q}_{0}

{\scriptstyle\maltese}

Lemma 30
.

S
is pre-ludicable.

Proof 5.6
.

Let
\kappa_{0}^{+}
be the first action of paths of
{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}
. We write
C
a positively saturated maximal clique of
S
. By lemma
28
, we can write
C=C_{1}\cup C^{\prime}C^{\prime\prime}
with properties as stated in this lemma.

•

By definition of
S
and the fact that a set of visitable paths of a behaviour is ludicable,
S
is prefix-closed and daimon-closed.

•

(positive saturation) Let
\mathpzc{r}
be a path of
S
:

–

Either
\mathpzc{r}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
. As
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
is ludicable, there exists a positively saturated maximal clique
C_{1}
for
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
such that
\mathpzc{r}\in C_{1}
. Let
C^{\prime\prime}
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
. Let us consider
C=C_{1}\cup(C_{1}\cap V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max})C^{\prime\prime}
. Then, by lemma
28
,
C
is a positively saturated maximal clique of
S
that contains
\mathpzc{r}
.

–

Or
\mathpzc{r}=\mathpzc{p}\mathpzc{q}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
. Let
C_{1}
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
that contains
\mathpzc{p}
and
C^{\prime\prime}
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
that contains
\kappa_{0}^{+}\mathpzc{q}
. Then, by lemma
28
, we remark that
C_{1}\cup(C_{1}\cap V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max})C^{\prime\prime}
is a positively saturated maximal clique of
S
that contains
\mathpzc{r}
.

•

(negative saturation)

Let
\mathpzc{r}\in S
and
\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}
be a legal path such that for all positively saturated maximal clique
C
of
S
, we have that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. We have to prove that
\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
:

–

Either
\mathpzc{r}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
:

If
\kappa^{-}
is an action appearing in
V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
, note that
\kappa^{-}
should be immediately justified by
\kappa_{0}^{+}
, hence
\kappa_{0}^{+}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{B}}}
.
Suppose that
\mathpzc{r}\not\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}
.
Let
C_{\mathpzc{r}}
be the clique for
S
as defined in proposition
6
: in particular
\mathpzc{r}\in C_{\mathpzc{r}}
. We remark that there is no
{\scriptstyle\maltese}
-free path
\mathpzc{q}
such that
\mathpzc{q}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}
and
\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{r}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}
thus there is no path
\mathpzc{q}\kappa^{-}
in
C_{\mathpzc{r}}
. It follows in particular that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{\mathpzc{r}}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\not\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
, contradiction. So
\mathpzc{r}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}
. Thereby
\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
.

Otherwise
\kappa^{-}
is an action appearing in
V_{{\mathbf{A}}}
. Let
C_{1}
(resp.
\kappa_{0}^{+}C^{\prime\prime}
) be a positively saturated maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
(resp. of
V_{{\mathbf{B}}_{[{\mathbf{A}}]}}
). Then
C=C_{1}\cup(C_{1}\cap V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max})C^{\prime\prime}
is a positively saturated maximal clique of
S
. Note that
\left<\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>=\left<\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{1}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>
hence, as
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
, we have that
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{1}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. So, as
V_{{\mathbf{A}}}
satisfies negative saturation,
\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
, thus
\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
.

–

Or
\mathpzc{r}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
:
\mathpzc{r}=\mathpzc{p}\mathpzc{q}
with
\mathpzc{p}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}
and
\mathpzc{q}\in V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
.

If
\kappa^{-}
is an action occurring in
V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
. Let
C_{1}
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
that contains
\mathpzc{p}
. Let
C^{\prime}=C_{1}\cap V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}
. Let
\kappa_{0}^{+}C^{\prime\prime}
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{B}}_{[{\mathbf{A}}]}}
. By lemma
28
,
C=C_{1}\cup C^{\prime}C^{\prime\prime}
is a positively saturated maximal clique of
S
. Hence
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. Note that
\left<\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>=\mathpzc{p}\left<\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C^{\prime\prime}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{q}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>
. Thus
\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C^{\prime\prime}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{q}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. Hence
\mathpzc{q}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{B}}}^{-}
as
V_{{\mathbf{B}}}
satisfies negative saturation. It follows that
\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in S
.

Otherwise
\kappa^{-}
is an action appearing in
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
. Let
C_{1}
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}
that contains
\mathpzc{p}
. Let
C^{\prime}=C_{1}\cap V_{{\mathbf{A}}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}}^{max}
. Let
\kappa_{0}^{+}C^{\prime\prime}
be a positively saturated maximal clique of
V_{{\mathbf{B}}_{[{\mathbf{A}}]}}
that contains
\kappa_{0}^{+}\mathpzc{q}
. By lemma
28
,
C=C_{1}\cup C^{\prime}C^{\prime\prime}
is a positively saturated maximal clique of
S
. Hence
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
. Note that
\left<\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{r}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>=\left<\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{1}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>
. Thus
\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{C_{1}}\raisebox{0.91092pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\overline{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{-}}}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}

.
∎

{defi}

Let
{\mathbf{A}}
and
{\mathbf{B}}
be behaviours,

•

{\mathbf{A}}^{+}=\{{\mathfrak{D}}[\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\ulcorner$}{\mathpzc{p}}\raisebox{-1.61685pt}{$\urcorner$}{\scriptstyle\maltese}/\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\ulcorner$}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}}\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\urcorner$}{\mathfrak{d}}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}\in V_{{\mathbf{A}}}^{max}]\penalty\ ;\penalty\ {\mathfrak{D}}\in{\mathbf{A}}\}

is obtained from
{\mathbf{A}}

{\mathbf{A}}

\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\ulcorner$}{\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}}\raisebox{2.03987pt}{$\urcorner$}{\mathfrak{d}}

\mathpzc{p}\kappa^{+}

.
|{\mathbf{A}}|^{+}

|{\mathbf{A}}|
.

•

|{\mathbf{A}}|

•

{\mathord{\mathchoice{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}}{\raise-0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\hbox{$\top$}\mkern-14.5mu\raise 0.3pt\hbox{$\top$}}{\mkern 4.0mu\raise-0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\raise 0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern 2.0mu}{\mkern 4.0mu\raise-0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern-14.0mu\raise 0.2pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\top$}\mkern 2.0mu}}}^{+}_{[{\mathbf{B}}]}=\{\{\kappa^{+}\}\penalty\ ;\penalty\ \kappa^{+}

6.
Conclusion

At first sight, Ludics objects seem to be easy to study: designs are nothing else but abstraction of proofs or counter-proofs of multiplicative-additive Linear Logic (MALL). However, this is not the case when one tries to identify among behaviours, i.e., closures of sets of designs, those that are interpretation of MALL formulas.
This paper is a first step toward a full algebraic study of behaviours. First, we make explicit the equivalence between the two presentations of a design, as set of paths versus set of chronicles.
We give a few properties concerning orthogonality in terms of path traversal, introducing visitable paths, i.e., paths that are visited by orthogonality.
Our main result is a characterization of finite MALL formulas, i.e., formulas built from the linear constants by means of additive and multiplicative connectives.
In particular, we show that such behaviours should be regular. Regularity is in fact a global property of visitable paths: roughly speaking, legal paths built from actions in the incarnation should be visitable.
Such a study should help understanding the structure of MALL proofs.
By contrast, many behaviours are not regular. We analyse one case of non-regularity: in short, a proof of

is a proof of
{\mathbf{A}}
followed by a proof of
{\mathbf{B}}
. We show that such a situation may be fully defined. This should be considered as a first step towards a full study of orientation in Ludics.

Let us remark finally that properties of Ludics that serve for proving that Ludics is a fully abstract model of (slightly modified polarized second-order) MALL, are satisfied for the entire Ludics and not only for behaviours interpreting MALL formulas: interaction between objects, that is cut-elimination, is at the heart of Ludics, thus it allows to consider the Ludics framework as a semantics for computation beyond what is given with MALL: a behaviour may model a type and (open) interaction between behaviours corresponds to composition of types. For future work, we plan to extend our analysis to the whole set of behaviours, defining a grammar for it in such a way that connectives of the grammar may be computationally (or logically) interpreted.

We thank anonymous referees for their thorough reviews and highly appreciate the comments and
suggestions.

A.1.
Ludics: Basic Definitions

{defi}

[Base]
A
base
is a non-empty finite set of sequents:
\Gamma_{1}\vdash\Delta_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{n}\vdash\Delta_{n}
such that each
\Delta_{j}
is a finite set of addresses, at most one
\Gamma_{i}
may be empty and the other
\Gamma_{i}
contain each exactly one address.
Furthermore if an address appears twice then one occurrence is in one of
\Gamma_{i}
of a sequent and the other in one of
\Delta_{j}
of another sequent, otherwise an address appears only once.

{defi}

action

\kappa

•

either a positive proper action
(+,\xi,I)
or a negative proper action
(-,\xi,I)
where the address
\xi
is said the focus of the action, and the finite set of integers
I
is said its ramification,

•

or the positive action daimon written
{\scriptstyle\maltese}
.

The notation
\overline{\kappa}
may be extended to sequences of actions

{defi}

[Chronicle]
A
chronicle

{\mathfrak{c}}
based on
\Gamma\vdash\Delta
is a non-empty and finite alternate sequence of actions such that

•

Positive proper action: A positive proper action is either justified, i.e., its focus is built by one of the previous actions in the sequence, or it is called initial.

•

Negative action: A negative action may be initial, in such a case it is the first action of the chronicle and its focus is in
\Gamma
. Otherwise it is justified by the immediate previous positive action.

•

Linearity: Actions have distinct foci.

•

Daimon: If present, a daimon ends the chronicle.

•

Polarity: If
\Gamma
is empty, the first action of
{\mathfrak{c}}
is positive, otherwise it is negative.

{defi}

[Coherence on Chronicles]
Two chronicles
{\mathfrak{c}}_{1}
and
{\mathfrak{c}}_{2}
are
coherent
, noted
{\mathfrak{c}}_{1}\coh{\mathfrak{c}}_{2}
, when the two following conditions are satisfied:

•

Comparability: Either one extends the other or they first differ on negative actions, i.e., if
w\kappa_{1}\coh w\kappa_{2}
then either
\kappa_{1}=\kappa_{2}
or
\kappa_{1}
and
\kappa_{2}
are negative actions.

•

Propagation: When they first differ on negative actions and these negative actions have distinct foci then the foci of following actions in
{\mathfrak{c}}_{1}
and
{\mathfrak{c}}_{2}
are pairwise distinct, i.e., if
w(-,\xi_{1},I_{1})w_{1}\kappa_{1}\coh w(-,\xi_{2},I_{2})w_{2}\kappa_{2}
with
\xi_{1}\neq\xi_{2}
then
\kappa_{1}
and
\kappa_{2}
have distinct foci.

{defi}

[Designs, Slices, Nets]
A
design

{\mathfrak{D}}
, based on
\Gamma\vdash\Delta
, is a set of chronicles based on
\Gamma\vdash\Delta
, such that the following conditions are satisfied:

•

Forest: The set of chronicles is prefix closed.

•

Coherence: The set is a clique of chronicles with respect to
\coh
.

•

Positivity: A chronicle without extension in
{\mathfrak{D}}
ends with a positive action.

•

Totality:
{\mathfrak{D}}
is non-empty when the base is positive, in that case all the chronicles begin with a (unique) positive action.

A
slice
is a design
{\mathfrak{S}}
such that if
w(-,\xi,I_{1}),w(-,\xi,I_{2})\in{\mathfrak{S}}
then
I_{1}=I_{2}
.

A
net
is a finite set of designs on disjoint bases.

A design is then a set of chronicles or a forest of actions (when one cares of justification between actions) that satisfies several constraints. It can also be presented as a sequent tree, however with ambiguity due to the possible weakening of addresses created by actions. We describe in example
A.1
a design based on
\vdash\xi
as a set of chronicles (on the left) and as a sequent tree (on the right):

{exa}

\begin{array}[]{cl}\{&(+,\xi,\{1,3\});\\
&(+,\xi,\{1,3\})(-,\xi.1,\{0\});\\
&(+,\xi,\{1,3\})(-,\xi.1,\{0\})(+,\xi.1.0,\{0\});\\
&(+,\xi,\{1,3\})(-,\xi.1,\{1\});\\
&(+,\xi,\{1,3\})(-,\xi.1,\{1\})(+,\xi.1.1,\{0\});\\
&(+,\xi,\{1,3\})(-,\xi.3,\{0\});\\
&(+,\xi,\{1,3\})(-,\xi.3,\{0\})(+,\xi.3.0,\emptyset)\,\,\,\,\}\end{array}

\textstyle\xi.1.0.0\vdash

\textstyle\vdash\xi.1.0

\textstyle\xi.1.1.0\vdash

\textstyle\vdash\xi.1.1

\textstyle\xi.1\vdash

\textstyle\vdash

\textstyle\vdash\xi.3.0

\textstyle\xi.3\vdash

\textstyle\vdash\xi

{defi}

[Closed cut-net]
A net of designs
{\mathfrak{R}}
is a
closed cut-net
if

•

addresses in bases are either distinct or present twice, once in a left part of a base and once in a right part of another base,

•

the net of designs is acyclic and connected with respect to the graph of bases and cuts.

An address present in a left part and in a right part defines a
cut
.
In a closed cut-net, the (unique) design whose base is positive is called the main design of the cut-net.

{defi}

[Interaction on closed cut-nets]
Let
{\mathfrak{R}}
be a closed cut-net.
The design resulting from the interaction, denoted by
[\![{\mathfrak{R}}]\!]
, is defined in the following way:
let
{\mathfrak{D}}
be the main design of
{\mathfrak{R}}
, with first action
\kappa
,

•

if
\kappa
is a daimon, then
[\![{\mathfrak{R}}]\!]=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}
,

•

otherwise
\kappa
is a proper positive action
(+,\sigma,I)
such that
\sigma
is part of a cut with another design with last rule
(-,\sigma,{\mathcal{N}})
(aggregating ramifications of actions with the same focus
\sigma
):

–

If
I\not\in\mathcal{N}
, then interaction fails.

–

Otherwise, interaction follows with the connected part of subdesigns obtained from
I
with the rest of
{\mathfrak{R}}
.

Following this definition, either interaction fails, or it does not end, or it results in the design
{\mathfrak{Dai}}=\{{\scriptstyle\maltese}\}
.
The definition of orthogonality follows:

{defi}

[Orthogonal, Behaviour]

•

Let
{\mathfrak{D}}
be a design of base

(resp.
\vdash\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{n}
),

.

{\mathrm{E}}
is a

.
A behaviour is positive (resp. negative) if the base of its designs is positive (resp. negative).

{\mathfrak{D}}
be a design, the

of
{\mathfrak{D}}
, written
{{\mathfrak{D}}}^{\scriptstyle\maltese}
,

.

.
Let us write

–

–

Otherwise
\alpha_{0}^{+}
is an action of
\mathpzc{q}_{0}
, then it is also the case for its justifier
\alpha_{1}^{-}
. If actions in
w^{\prime\prime}
are actions of
\mathpzc{q}_{0}
, we define
\mathpzc{r}_{1}
,
\mathpzc{q}_{1}
,
\mathpzc{p}_{1}
as before and this yields a contradiction. Else let
\beta^{+}
be the last action of
\mathpzc{p}_{0}
in
w^{\prime\prime}
. There is also an action
\gamma^{-}
of
{\mathpzc{p}}_{0}
which immediately precedes
\beta^{+}
in
w^{\prime\prime}
.
One can delete from
\mathpzc{r}_{0}
the actions
\gamma^{-}
and
\beta^{+}
.
Then we get a shorter sequence
\mathpzc{r}_{1}
together with paths
\mathpzc{p}_{1}
and
\mathpzc{q}_{1}
such that
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[10.0417pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.44444pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{658093}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{658093}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{658093}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{658093}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}$}}}{\makebox[10.0417pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.44444pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{658093}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{658093}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{658093}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{658093}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}$}}}{\makebox[8.31952pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.41112pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{545228}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{545228}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{545228}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{545228}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}$}}}{\makebox[7.6529pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{1.72221pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{501540}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{501540}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{501540}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{501540}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{p}_{1}}}$}}}}
is not a path. Hence a contradiction with the hypothesis of minimality.
∎

We prove now proposition
22
that characterizes, in the general case, the visitable paths of a tensor. This is a generalization of what was at stake for proving that the tensor is stable for regularity (proposition
21
).
We decompose the proof in two lemmas as each of them is quite long and technical (lemmas
36
and
37
).
In each lemma, we need associativity of interaction in terms of paths (lemma
35
). Associativity of interaction in terms of designs is proved in
[
Gir01
]
.
This initial lemma uses a notion of projection:

{defi}
[Projection]
Let
\mathpzc{p}
be a path, the projection of
\mathpzc{p}
on
X
, written
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\mathpzc{p}\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!X}{\mathpzc{p}\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!X}{\mathpzc{p}\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0muX}{\mathpzc{p}\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!X}}
, is the subsequence of
\mathpzc{p}
made of actions of
X
,
X
being a set of actions, a path, a design or a net.

Lemma 35
.

Let
{\mathfrak{R}}
,
{\mathfrak{S}}
,
{\mathfrak{T}}
be three nets of designs such that
{\mathfrak{S}}
and
{\mathfrak{T}}
have distinct bases and
[\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}},{\mathfrak{T}}]\!]={\scriptstyle\maltese}
,
then
\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>=\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}
.

Proof A.2
.

The proof is done by induction on the length of
\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>
. Note first that each proper step of normalization occurs between a subnet of
{\mathfrak{R}}
and either a subnet of
{\mathfrak{S}}
or a subnet of
{\mathfrak{T}}
as
{\mathfrak{S}}
and
{\mathfrak{T}}
have distinct bases.

If
\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>=\epsilon
then
{\mathfrak{R}}={\scriptstyle\maltese}
thus
[\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]={\scriptstyle\maltese}
hence
\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>=\epsilon
. The result follows.

Suppose the property satisfied for lengths less or equal to
n
and
\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>
has length
n+1
. We consider the various cases:

•

If
{\mathfrak{S}}
is positive:
{\mathfrak{S}}=(+,\sigma,I){\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}
.

Then
{\mathfrak{R}}=(-,\sigma,I){\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{J\neq I}(-,\sigma,J){\mathfrak{R}}_{J}\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K){\mathfrak{R}}_{\xi,K}
.

Let
{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K){\mathfrak{R}}_{\xi,K}
:

–

[\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]=[\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}]\!]
then

\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>=\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}]\!]\right>

–

\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>=(+,\sigma,I)\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime}\right>
then

\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}=\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}

thus the result by induction hypothesis.

•

If
{\mathfrak{R}}
is positive:

–

If
{\mathfrak{R}}=(+,\sigma,I){\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}
and
{\mathfrak{S}}=(-,\sigma,I){\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{J\neq I}(-,\sigma,J){\mathfrak{S}}_{J}\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K){\mathfrak{S}}_{\xi,K}
. Let
{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K){\mathfrak{S}}_{\xi,K}
:

*

[\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]=[\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime\prime}]\!]
then

\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>=\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime\prime}]\!]\right>

*

\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>=(-,\sigma,I)\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>
then

\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}=\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}^{\prime\prime}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}

thus the result by induction hypothesis.

–

If
{\mathfrak{R}}=(+,\sigma,I){\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}
and
{\mathfrak{T}}=(-,\sigma,I){\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{J\neq I}(-,\sigma,J){\mathfrak{T}}_{J}\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K){\mathfrak{T}}_{\xi,K}
. Let
{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K){\mathfrak{T}}_{\xi,K}
:

*

[\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]=(+,\sigma,I)[\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]

then
\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>=\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!(+,\sigma,I)[\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>=(-,\sigma,I)\left<{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>

*

\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>=(-,\sigma,I)\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>

then
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}=\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}=\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}}}

thus the result by induction hypothesis.

•

If
{\mathfrak{R}}
and
{\mathfrak{S}}
are negative, hence
{\mathfrak{T}}
is positive: let
{\mathfrak{T}}=(+,\sigma,I){\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime}
and
{\mathfrak{R}}=(-,\sigma,I){\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{J\neq I}(-,\sigma,J){\mathfrak{R}}_{J}\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K){\mathfrak{R}}_{\xi,K}
.

Let
{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K){\mathfrak{R}}_{\xi,K}
:

–

[\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]=(-,\sigma,I)[\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\cup\bigcup_{J\neq I}(-,\sigma,J)[\![{\mathfrak{R}}_{J},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\cup\bigcup_{\xi\neq\sigma,K}(-,\xi,K)[\![{\mathfrak{R}}_{\xi,K},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]
then

\left<{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>=(-,\sigma,I)\left<{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{S}}]\!]\right>

–

\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>=(-,\sigma,I)\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>

then
\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}=\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}}}=\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\mkern 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}}{\left<{\mathfrak{S}}{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{R}}^{\prime}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!{\mathfrak{T}}^{\prime\prime}}}

thus the result by induction hypothesis.
∎

Indeed, for each negative action that occurs in
\left<{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{1}{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{2}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{E}}^{\prime}\right>
and is an address in
{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{1}
(resp.
{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{2}
), then the next action in
\left<{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{1}{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{2}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!{\mathfrak{E}}^{\prime}\right>
is positive and should also be an address in
{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{1}
(resp.
{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{2}
) as in a path a positive action is in the same chronicle as the negative action that precedes it, hence also in an interaction path.

•

Furthermore following the adjunction theorem (
[
Gir01
]
, Th. 14),
we have that

(-,\xi,I)[\![{\mathfrak{E}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{2}]\!]\cup{\mathfrak{E}}^{\prime\prime}\in{\mathbf{P}}^{\perp}.

Remark finally that
\left<{\mathfrak{D}}_{1}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!(-,\xi,I)[\![{\mathfrak{E}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{D}}_{2}]\!]\cup{\mathfrak{E}}^{\prime\prime}\right>=(+,\xi,I)\left<{\mathfrak{D}}^{\prime}_{1}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{E}}^{\prime},{\mathfrak{D}}_{2}]\!]\right>=(+,\xi,I)\mathpzc{r}_{1}
.
Thus
(+,\xi,I)\mathpzc{r}_{1}\in V_{{\mathbf{P}}}
. Similarly,
(+,\xi,J)\mathpzc{r}_{2}\in V_{{\mathbf{Q}}}
.

Hence by lemma
35
,

\left<\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{s}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}]\!]\right>=\mathinner{\mathchoice{\left<\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\otimes\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{s}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}}{\left<\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\otimes\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{s}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern- 1.0mu\upharpoonright\mkern 1.0mu\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}}{\left<\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\otimes\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{s}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\right>\!\!\upharpoonright\!\!\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}}}=\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}
.

Thus
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset[\![\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{s}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}]\!]
. Hence, as there are no other actions with subaddresses of
\xi.i
for

in
[\![\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{s}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}]\!]
, we have that
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}=[\![\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{s}_{1}}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}]\!]
.

–

Furthermore, as
\overline{\mathpzc{s}}
is a path of
\raisebox{0.52205pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\mathinner{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.91667pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.44444pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{256683}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{256683}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{256683}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{256683}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{r}}}$}}}{\makebox[3.91667pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{3.44444pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{256683}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{256683}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{256683}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{3.44444pt}{$\resizebox{256683}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\mathpzc{r}}}$}}}{\makebox[3.12502pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{2.41112pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{204801}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{204801}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{204801}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{2.41112pt}{$\resizebox{204801}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptstyle\mathpzc{r}}}$}}}{\makebox[2.70836pt][c]{\mbox{\rule{0.0pt}{1.72221pt}$\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{177495}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{177495}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{177495}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{r}}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\raisebox{1.72221pt}{$\resizebox{177495}{0}{$\sim$}$}\hss}{\scriptscriptstyle\mathpzc{r}}}$}}}}\,}\raisebox{0.52205pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
, we have that
\overline{\mathpzc{s}}
is a path of
{\mathfrak{R}}_{1}
, hence also
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{s}_{1}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset{\mathfrak{R}}_{1}
.

Normalization being deterministic, we have then that
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}\subset[\![{\mathfrak{R}}_{1},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}]\!]
.

–

Recall that
[\![{\mathfrak{D}}_{1},\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}]\!]={\scriptstyle\maltese}
, more precisely that
\mathpzc{v}_{1}=\left<{\mathfrak{D}}_{1}\!\!\leftarrow\!\!\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}_{1}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\right>
. And that
[\![{\mathfrak{D}}_{1},{\mathfrak{R}}_{1},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}]\!]={\scriptstyle\maltese}
.

With the previous item, it follows that the path
\mathpzc{v}_{1}
is a prefix of
\left<{\mathfrak{D}}_{1}\!\!\leftarrow\!\![\![{\mathfrak{R}}_{1},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}]\!]\right>
.

–

Finally,
\overline{\mathpzc{v}_{1}\kappa^{-}}
is a path of
[\![{\mathfrak{R}}_{1},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}]\!]
. Hence, for the normalization between
{\mathfrak{D}}_{1}
and
[\![{\mathfrak{R}}_{1},\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{q}^{\prime}_{1}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}]\!]
to converge, we should also have
\mathpzc{v}_{1}\kappa^{-}
to be a path of
{\mathfrak{D}}_{1}
, i.e.,
\mathpzc{v}\kappa^{-}
to be a path of
{\mathfrak{D}}
.

–

Contradiction with the hypothesis
{\mathfrak{D}}\not\perp\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}\kappa^{-}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}
.
Thus
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}\kappa^{-}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\in{\mathbf{P}}^{\perp}
.

As
\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}}\raisebox{1.59543pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\in{\mathbf{P}}
and
\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\ulcorner\mkern-6.0mu\ulcorner\mkern-2.0mu$}{\,\overline{\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}\kappa^{-}}\,}\raisebox{-0.24463pt}{$\mkern-2.0mu\urcorner\mkern-6.0mu\urcorner$}^{c}\in{\mathbf{P}}^{\perp}
, we have that
\mathpzc{p}^{\prime}\kappa^{-}{\scriptstyle\maltese}\in V_{{\mathbf{P}}}
.
∎

. We use the following notations:
